title: DeepMind: AI agents find two new attacks on legacy 1024-bit RSA
subtitle: Working under human cryptanalysts, DeepMind's agents sped up signature forgery by roughly 1,600x and cut batch factoring cost by 30x — against a key length already deprecated.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google DeepMind on November 6 announced two new cryptanalytic results against 1024-bit RSA, produced by AI agents working under the supervision of cryptographers Nadia Heninger and Emmanuel Thomé. The DeepMind team was led by Dj Dvijotham and Abhradeep Thakurta. One attack targets signature forgery — when an attacker controls roughly half the signed message, a new algorithm is about 1,600 times faster than the previous best, though DeepMind flags the figure as a theoretical bound for the shortest signed inputs. The second attack lowers the average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key in a batch by about 30x over prior methods. Modern RSA-2048 is not affected.

The newsworthy part is not that 1024-bit RSA is broken — NIST deprecated it years ago — but that AI agents, used as cryptanalysis collaborators rather than tools, produced novel algorithmic improvements in a field where every speedup is typically a human career's work. The agents did not run autonomously: Heninger and Thomé framed the problems, checked the math, and iterated with the models over months. The result is a credible existence proof that AI agents can compress parts of a research cycle that used to take years.

The timing matters. Post-quantum migration programs across governments and financial systems have been budgeted around the assumption that classical cryptanalysis of RSA improves slowly and predictably. If AI-accelerated cryptanalysis closes gaps faster than planned, 2048-bit margins look thinner — not broken, but less comfortable. The results also land the day after OpenAI launched GPT-6 Cyber, which claimed step-function gains in offensive security capability. Together, they suggest frontier labs are now competing on applied cryptography as a capability benchmark.

A takeaway for learners: in security research, the headline number is almost never the full story. The 1,600x figure is for a narrow adversary model against a key length nobody should still be using. Reading the primary source — DeepMind's technical post and the underlying paper — is how you learn to tell a demonstration from a deployment-blocking result. Train that habit now; it will matter more as more labs publish AI-assisted research.
